newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba repo move seen as sign of steady rates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba repo move seen as sign of steady rates.

text.p: The Bundesbank made a large injection of funds into the German money market on Wednesday in what dealers interpreted as a sign it did not want to raise short-term interest rates for the time being.

The central bank added a net 2.6 billion marks ($1.4 billion) at its weekly auction for securities repurchase agreements, or repos -- its principal means of supplying the money market with funds -- at a fixed repo rate of 3.00 percent.

Traders had speculated the bank might prepare the ground for higher money-market rates by keeping the market short of liquidity. Speculation had mounted that the Bundesbank may be forced to raise rates in defence of the weakening mark.
But Wednesday's move appeared to dampen those expectations.

"The Bundesbank apparently does not want higher rates," one money market dealer said. "It appears to want to remain with fixed rate repos at 3.00 percent. But things may look different next week if the dollar rises above 1.90 marks."
Several dealers predicted the Bundesbank would set further repo tenders at a fixed rate of 3.00 percent -- the rate that has prevailed since August 1996.
The repo news helped push the mark down to its lowest level against the dollar in nearly eight years for the fourth consecutive trading day. The dollar was trading at 1.8860 marks at 0915 GMT.

Markets have speculated the Bundesbank may signal higher interest rates by switching from fixed-rate repo tenders -- at which it sets the rate itself -- to variable-rate tenders, at which the repo rate is determined by the rates at which banks bid for Bundesbank funds.

A heavy drain of funds from the money market on Wednesday might have been interpreted as a sign the Bundesbank was preparing it for a return to variable-rate tenders and encouraging banks to bid the repo rate higher next week.

The Bundesbank's last central bank council meeting before its one-month summer break on July 24 took the unusual step of setting fixed-rate repo tenders for just two weeks, even though the council was only due to reconvene after four weeks.

The second of those weekly repo pacts was allocated on Wednesday, leaving markets in the dark as to whether next week's repo tender will be a fixed-rate repo at 3.00 percent, a variable-rate repo, or a fixed-rate repo at a higher rate.
Theoretically, the Bundesbank does not have to say what form the tender will take until it invites bids from banks for repos next Tuesday.
But with markets speculating feverishly about whether the Bundesbank will shift to higher rates, the bank may make an announcement sooner, dealers said.

"I wouldn't be surprised if the Bundesbank waits until next Tuesday to announce what form the repo tender will take but it could be that the Bundesbank will make an announcement on Thursday to deflate market speculation," one dealer said.
But analysts doubt whether a return to variable rate repos with the likely effect of a slight rise in the repo rate to 3.10 percent or so would be enough to underpin the mark.

In addition, with unemployment high, no sign of imminent inflation increases and consumer spending still largely stagnant, many analysts believe the Bundesbank has no need yet to usher in a cycle of interest rate increases.
Money market rates for overnight funds were quoted in a range of 3.00 to 3.10 percent on Wednesday, little changed from 3.05/10 percent on Tuesday.
The Bundesbank on Wednesday allotted a total of 74.7 billion marks in one-week funds to the money market, taking eligible securities as collateral.
A repo pact totalling 72.1 billion marks expired on Wednesday so the repo allocation meant that a net 2.6 billion marks flowed into the money market.

One dealer said the net addition of repo funds came as no surprise after a steep fall in commercial banks' deposits with the central bank on Tuesday -- a sign of liquidity shortage in the money market.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
($ = 1.877 German Marks)
